target_customer: Busy urban women who get regular blowouts, and partner salons with open chairs
problem: Women wanted fast, affordable, last minute blowouts without booking hassle, and salons had unused capacity.
business_model: Monthly membership for blowouts (99 dollars unlimited in 2015, tiered after) with a per-service fee paid to partner salons

founders.name: Alanna Gregory
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch May 2015 quotes her saying she was working on Wall Street before starting Vive. YC page says she is now managing partner at Constellation, a growth consultancy.

exit.reason: No shutdown or sale announcement found; the YC page uses past tense for the founder role.

competitors.name: Drybar
competitors.what: Blowout bar chain; the founder said she would like Drybar as a client
competitors.traction_then: Chain of storefronts limited by how many it can open, per the founder

technical_complexity.rationale: Booking, payments and salon scheduling are standard app work; partner onboarding was the harder operational part.

defensibility.rationale: A salon network helped, but ClassPass style models were copyable and the TechCrunch article called the model almost identical to ClassPass.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Not documented. Drybar launched an in-home app in 2015 per a search summary.

market_need_then: TechCrunch in May 2015 reported 66 partner salons in Manhattan and the founder's claim that users who got one or two blowouts a month moved to about weekly use; by Feb 2016 more than 34,000 appointments and 230 salons were reported.

identity.voice_and_tone: Positioned as a modern beauty concierge and the ClassPass for hair

branding.brand_signature: Modern beauty concierge for the modern woman; unlimited blowouts
branding.community_and_virality: Covered by Fortune, Business Insider, Time Out, TechCrunch and others in 2015 and 2016, and a Business Insider headline said women were going nuts for the offer.

brand_strength.rationale: Broad consumer press and a catchy ClassPass for blowouts framing, but the name is generic and shares search results with the HTC Vive headset.

outcome_analysis: Vive sold a subscription for blowouts across partner salons, reached New York, Chicago and later Los Angeles, and raised about 2.3 million dollars in a February 2016 seed after earlier friends, family and angel money of just over 1 million dollars. It is marked inactive and the founder moved on to a consultancy, but no source states when or why it ended, so the cause is not public and failure factors stay empty.
notes: The company website field in the shard is empty so no site was fetched. The 2015-08 seed rests on a single database (CB Insights lists seed rounds dated 2015-05-21 and 2015-08-19 without amounts, total 2.76 million over 5 rounds); an Xconomy 120,000 dollar seed item dated 2015-08-19 has a Boulder address and may be another company, so no amount or investor is recorded. TechCrunch May 2015 says just over 1 million dollars was raised from friends and family plus a small angel round, not recorded as a round since no date. The Drybar mention is from the founder's own quote; other rivals such as Glamsquad and Vensette appear in undated or later articles and are not listed. Searches for the shutdown returned HTC Vive results only.
